opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's going to get a lot more interesting. Nvidia has done an incredible job, and it's not just the hardware. It's the whole stack: CUDA, the libraries, the networking, and the fact that every researcher learned on their GPUs. That ecosystem advantage is real, and it doesn't disappear overnight.

But I think the landscape is shifting, for a few reasons.

First, the workloads have consolidated. Ten years ago you had CNNs, RNNs, all sorts of architectures, and you needed very flexible hardware and software. Now most of the compute goes to transformers, or transformer-like models, and a handful of operations: matrix multiplies, attention, some memory-bound pieces. When the workload is that concentrated, it's much easier for a competitor to say, "We don't need to support everything. We just need to be really good at these few kernels." That lowers the barrier a lot.

Second, inference is becoming the dominant cost. Training is still huge, but serving these models to many users, especially with reasoning models generating long chains of tokens, is where much of the spend is going. Inference has different bottlenecks. It's often limited by memory bandwidth rather than raw FLOPs, and latency matters a lot. That opens room for different designs, whether that's AMD with lots of HBM, or startups doing more specialized architectures with lots of on-chip SRAM.

Third, the software moat is eroding somewhat. Many people now write kernels in higher-level tools like Triton, or in other DSLs that can target multiple backends. And frameworks like PyTorch are increasingly hardware-agnostic. I've worked on low-level kernels for a long time, and I've noticed that the abstractions are getting better. Once you write something at a slightly higher level, porting it to new hardware becomes weeks of work instead of years. AI itself is starting to help with kernel writing too, which could speed this up further.

So my view over the next couple of years: Nvidia stays dominant, especially for frontier training, because scale-out networking and reliability at tens of thousands of chips is really hard. But I expect real share to go to AMD, to the hyperscalers' in-house chips like TPUs and Trainium, and to some inference-focused players. Customers want a second source. They want price pressure. And the biggest buyers can afford to invest in the software to make alternatives work.

The part I find most exciting as a researcher is the co-design. Hardware shapes which algorithms win. Attention took off partly because it maps well onto GPUs. If hardware diversifies, we might see architectures that are better suited to different chips, and that feedback loop between models and hardware could drive a lot of progress.

r001.rationale: It attributes Nvidia’s advantage to its ecosystem, including CUDA, libraries, networking, and researcher familiarity.

r002.rationale: It says compute has concentrated around transformers and a few operations, making it easier for competitors to optimize for those workloads.

r003.rationale: It cites AMD’s large HBM capacity as an alternative suited to inference’s memory-bandwidth demands.

r004.rationale: It says scale-out networking is difficult at very large chip counts, identifying it as a major challenge for frontier training.

r005.rationale: It predicts Nvidia will retain dominance while AMD, hyperscaler chips, and inference-focused players gain share over the next couple of years.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think it's useful to separate a few things, because "competition with Nvidia" means different things depending on which part of the stack you're looking at.

On the hardware side, the gap is narrowing faster than people expected. If you look at AMD's MI300 and MI350 series, on raw specs — memory bandwidth, HBM capacity, FLOPs — they're genuinely competitive, and in some cases ahead. And then you have the hyperscalers doing their own silicon: Google with TPUs, which have been around for years and are very mature, Amazon with Trainium, Microsoft and Meta with their own efforts. So the question isn't really whether anyone can build a chip that's competitive on paper. People can.

The harder part is the software, and that's where I spend most of my time. Nvidia's real moat has always been CUDA and the ecosystem around it — cuBLAS, cuDNN, NCCL, all of that — plus the fact that every researcher has been writing CUDA kernels for fifteen years. When I wrote FlashAttention, I wrote it for Nvidia GPUs first because that's where the users were and where the tooling was most mature. Getting the same performance on a different chip isn't just recompiling; you have to understand the memory hierarchy, the warp or wavefront structure, how to do asynchronous copies, and you often have to rewrite the hot kernels from scratch.

What's changing is that the workloads have consolidated. A couple of years ago, you had this enormous variety of model architectures and every lab was doing something different. Now, the dominant workload is pretty clear: transformer training and inference, with attention, matrix multiplies, and a handful of other ops. If you only need to be really good at maybe ten kernels, that's a tractable problem for a competitor. You don't need the entire CUDA ecosystem; you need those ten kernels to be fast and the communication layer to be solid. And I think that's exactly what AMD, Google, and the others have figured out.

Inference in particular is where I expect competition to get real first. Training is extremely demanding — you need large, tightly coupled clusters, interconnect matters enormously, and you're very sensitive to any numerical weirdness. Inference is more forgiving. The workload is more predictable, you care a lot about memory bandwidth and cost per token, and you can run on a smaller unit of compute. So I think over the next couple of years you'll see a meaningful chunk of inference move to non-Nvidia hardware, because the economics are too compelling and the software burden is smaller.

The other thing I'd point to is the compiler and DSL layer. Projects like Triton, and things we and others are working on around higher-level abstractions for writing kernels, mean that you can increasingly write performance-critical code once and target multiple backends. It's not fully there — you still lose performance on the long tail — but the direction is clear. Every bit of portability at that layer erodes the lock-in.

That said, I don't want to oversell it. Nvidia isn't standing still. Blackwell and what comes after are very good, their interconnect story with NVLink is hard to match, and they have a decade head start on making everything just work. I think the realistic picture is not that Nvidia loses, but that the market goes from basically a monopoly to something more like a strong leader with credible alternatives, especially on inference. And honestly, from the perspective of someone who works on efficiency, that's a healthy outcome — it pushes everyone to optimize, and it means the hardware roadmap gets shaped by more than one company's priorities.

r001.rationale: It identifies CUDA and Nvidia’s surrounding software ecosystem as Nvidia’s real moat.

r002.rationale: It says workloads have consolidated around transformers and a small set of operations, making it tractable for competitors to optimize their chips for those workloads.

r003.rationale: It says AMD’s HBM capacity is competitive on paper, but does not identify larger memory capacity as an inference advantage.

r004.rationale: It says training requires tightly coupled clusters and that interconnect matters enormously, identifying connectivity as a major training constraint.

r005.rationale: It predicts that a meaningful chunk of inference will move to non-Nvidia hardware over the next couple of years.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s going to be difficult to compete with Nvidia by just building a chip with better specs. The hardware matters, but so much of the value is in the software ecosystem—how easy it is to take an existing model, get it running, and actually get good performance.

When you look at a new accelerator, the peak FLOPS might look great. But can you use those FLOPS? Do you have the right kernels? What happens when the architecture changes and you need a new operation? That’s where having a mature ecosystem and lots of people who know how to program it is a big advantage.

Over the next couple of years, I’d expect competitors to find traction in specific workloads, especially inference, where you can target a relatively well-defined problem and compete on cost or power efficiency. Training is harder because you need flexibility, and you need a lot of chips to work together reliably.

I’m hopeful that better compilers and more portable programming tools will make it easier to support multiple types of hardware. But that takes time. So I’d expect incremental progress from competitors rather than a sudden shift away from Nvidia.

r001.rationale: The response says Nvidia’s mature software ecosystem and programming base give it a major advantage over chip competitors.

r002.rationale: It does not describe AI workloads converging around transformer-like architectures or explain how that convergence makes chips easier to design.

r003.rationale: It does not mention AMD or larger memory capacity as an inference advantage.

r004.rationale: It says training requires many chips to work together reliably, but does not identify networking as a major bottleneck.

r005.rationale: It predicts competitors will gain traction in specific workloads and expects programming tools to support multiple hardware types over the next couple of years.

sol-6.1.text:
I think Nvidia will remain very strong over the next couple of years. The challenge for competitors is that they’re competing with an entire software ecosystem, not just a chip. You can have impressive hardware specs, but people need to be able to run their models efficiently without spending months rewriting everything.

The opening, I think, is in more specific workloads, especially inference. If you know exactly what model you’re serving and what your latency requirements are, there’s room to build something that’s more cost-effective. Training is harder because the workloads keep changing, and flexibility matters a lot.

So I’d watch how easy these alternatives become to program. Can a small team get good performance on them? That’s a much stronger signal than peak FLOPS. Competition will grow, but turning good hardware into something people can actually use is going to take time.

r001.rationale: The response says Nvidia competes with an entire software ecosystem, not just a chip, and connects that ecosystem to the difficulty competitors face.

r002.rationale: It discusses inference and training workloads but does not say that AI workloads are converging around transformer architectures or that this makes chip design easier.

r003.rationale: It mentions cost-effective inference opportunities but does not identify AMD or memory capacity as an advantage.

r004.rationale: It does not identify networking as a bottleneck for AI training.

r005.rationale: It predicts growing competition and discusses alternatives, but does not predict workloads running across different chip vendors within the next couple of years.
